As cheap capital recedes and artificial intelligence intensifies competition for technical talent, computing capacity, and executive attention, BCG argues that capital allocation alone can no longer secure value creation. CEOs must manage every constrained resource as an integrated portfolio of investment and execution choices.

Execution capacity is becoming the binding constraintWhile 33% of investors now rank return on capital as their top priority, funding alone cannot deliver AI or transformation plans without scarce skills, technology capacity, and leadership attention.

Invisible constraints can destroy value faster than capital shortfallsAt one bank, executives sponsored eight to ten projects each; managing work against fixed capacity raised on-target delivery from 35%–45% to more than 80%.

Strategy must be tested against all resources required to execute itLeaders should work backward from priorities, specifying demands for capital, talent, specialist skills, technology, and change capacity before committing. Otherwise, funded projects can still fail for lack of execution support.

Resource allocation must become a continuous, enterprise-wide disciplineRather than letting functions negotiate separately, CEOs should repeatedly reallocate resources toward the highest-value opportunities. Initiatives must earn continued access, especially when they consume scarce leadership attention.

Rarely has the pursuit of value creation been more demanding, or the margin for error so unforgiving. The era of cheap capital is over. AI is creating unprecedented demand for scarce technical expertise and compute. Even C-suite bandwidth is in shorter supply, with 60% of CEOs saying that near-term issues consume an outsized share of their time.Value creation has always been a multidimensional challenge because multiple scarce resources drive it. In years past, however, CEOs could work around constraints on execution capacity, such as talent shortages, by tapping one resource: capital. When it was cheap and abundant, companies could spend their way around constraints elsewhere. But tectonic shifts in the business landscape are stripping away that flexibility. As the cost of capital climbs, investors become more focused on how it’s deployed. In BCG’s latest Global Investor Survey, some 33% of respondents ranked return on capital as their top investment priority—an eight-percentage-point increase in just two years.Effective capital allocation is nonnegotiable for value creation, but it’s only one variable. To excel in a world where any scarce resource can derail even the best plan, CEOs must look across the totality of what drives value (e.g., capital, capabilities, talent, and leadership attention). They then need to actively manage all of these scarce resources in concert across their portfolio of strategic priorities, ensuring that each has both the investment capacity and the execution capacity required to deliver value.Getting to grips with that broader, deeper portfolio logic starts with understanding how resource constraints have evolved. From there, CEOs need to assess what each strategic priority demands from each scarce resource, and then manage them across the portfolio, over time, to continuously optimize value.

Five CEO Moves to Unlock Superior Value Creation Through Holistic Resource Management

Holistic Resource Management
Capital remains a critical limiting factor in value creation, but it is no longer the only one. In many organizations, the binding constraint is increasingly execution capacity.AI, for example, opens pathways to extraordinary opportunities. But it also forces difficult choices about where limited technical talent and tokens (the basic units of data that AI models use and AI providers charge for) can drive the greatest value. AI initiatives also compete for technology capacity and leadership attention—resources that capital alone cannot always compensate for.Navigating this evolving map of scarcity requires a broader portfolio logic that we call Holistic Resource Management: applying the same disciplined value creation logic that guides capital allocation across every scarce resource and across the portfolio of strategic priorities that compete for them.Capital gets scrutinized because every dollar is measured. The same cannot be said, however, of other constrained resources. Too often, they are left to be contested across the organization, with allocation driven more by bargaining power than value creation measured with a common currency. Without that discipline, companies can fall into the trap of spreading resources evenly rather than strategically (See the sidebar “When Management Bandwidth Is the Constraint”). They might double down on today’s cash generators while starving tomorrow’s growth engines. Value-draining businesses with little future growth potential can escape scrutiny, and promising businesses that suffer temporary setbacks can get cut off prematurely.

When Management Bandwidth Is the Constraint

At one major bank, an activity survey found that executives were sponsoring eight to ten projects on average, while managers were working on five, with 34% juggling seven or more. By measuring that load and managing the initiative portfolio against a fixed capacity, the bank increased the share of projects delivering on their stated objectives from 35%–45% to more than 80%.

Over time, poor resource allocation can lead to a value-eroding initiative sprawl that nobody deliberately designed but CEOs may struggle to unwind (See the sidebar “When the Constraint Is Invisible”).

When the Constraint Is Invisible

At one industrial company, everyone assumed capital was the scarce resource. It was management attention. A handful of failing businesses, each one a rounding error on the top line, had somehow captured an enormous share of the leadership team’s time, pulling the best executives into meetings about problems that were never going to be solved.On a capital basis, those businesses looked harmless enough. On a scarcity basis, they were the most expensive things the company owned. Shutting them down released almost no money, but it did free up the attention, talent, and energy that had been the real brake on growth all along. Return on management bandwidth is the calculation almost nobody bothers to run.

Holistic Resource Management avoids this trap by looking at the organization’s strategic priorities, growth initiatives, and operational commitments as a whole, not in isolation. Leaders assess what each requires in terms of capital, capabilities, leadership attention, technology, and other scarce resources. Crucially, decisions about where those resources should go are not made function by function. Leaders across the enterprise make those choices together, evaluating initiatives by the value they create—or could create—relative to the scarce resources they consume.This shifts the fundamental question leaders collectively ask from “Is this business profitable?” to “Is this the best use of our constrained resources to create value today and drive growth tomorrow?”Done well, Holistic Resource Management not only changes how companies create value but how the market values them. Activist investors rarely target companies randomly. They tend to surface when scarce resources are being committed to businesses and initiatives that fail to create value.

Five CEO Moves to Unlock Superior Value Creation Through Holistic Resource Management
Holistic Resource Management is not a one-time planning exercise or a new budgeting process. It is a management discipline for continuously aligning scarce resources with the opportunities that create the greatest value. The following five actions provide a practical way to approach it:Map all constraints, not just capitalEffective resource allocation starts with a complete view of scarcity. Most organizations know exactly where their financial capital is deployed. But they often have far less visibility into the resources that increasingly constrain execution.To understand where those constraints lie, they must build an inventory of every material constraint—capital, talent, scarce skills (e.g., AI, quantum, regulatory), leadership bandwidth, token consumption, and change absorption capacity. They then need to measure and manage each with the same rigor they apply to financial capital.Ensure strategy is executableStrategies fail when organizations commit to goals they lack the capacity to deliver. CEOs and their teams should start by working backward from strategy. That means defining what every priority requires—in capital, capabilities, leadership attention, technology, and other scarce resources—before committing to execution. Leaders can then test those demands against the organization’s available execution capacity and make the necessary trade-offs to maximize value.Drive trade-offs through strategy, not silosMost organizations optimize scarce resources one at a time. Capital allocation happens in one process, talent planning in another, token budgeting in a third, and so on. The trade-offs between them are rarely reconciled. The result is predictable: projects are fully funded but starved of talent or have the engineering capacity to deliver but not the leadership attention to absorb the change.Holistic Resource Management brings those decisions together. The question is no longer whether an initiative is funded, but whether the organization has all of the resources required to execute its highest-value bets.Manage against what’s limiting value creationResource decisions begin by identifying the binding constraint that determines what the organization can actually deliver. It may be capital. But it could be engineering capacity, or leadership attention.Whatever it is, when organizations manage resources against the real constraint rather than simply against the budget, they make better trade-offs, and ultimately better value creation bets.Reallocate continuously and make it countThe map of scarcity is constantly evolving. Resources that are abundant today can become tomorrow’s binding constraint. Resource allocation therefore cannot be confined to an annual budgeting exercise. It requires regular reassessment, with the flexibility to redirect scarce resources and reshape the initiative portfolio as conditions change.That discipline only works if resources must be earned, rather than inherited. Strategic priorities and initiatives that no longer justify their consumption of scarce resources—including, and especially, leadership attention—should lose access to them.

The era of cheap capital is gone, taking with it the option to paper over poor management of other scarce resources. As the map of scarcity continues to evolve, the CEOs who outperform will be those who apply the same discipline and rigor once reserved for capital across every scarce resource. They will make better-informed bets—and improve the odds that those bets create lasting value.
